clue.text: Going up a trail

parts.note: a scent is the trail an animal leaves for hounds to follow

explanation.surface: Someone is climbing a path up a hill.
explanation.definitionFit: An ascent is a climb, the act of rising or moving upward.

clue.text: He flew in from Barcelona via Torremolinos

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run of words that follows, spanning Barcelona, via and Torremolinos

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker flew in on a hop between two Spanish resorts.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilot is someone who flies an aircraft; the clue's 'He flew' describes such a person.

clue.text: Gathered together various beldames and old Bob

indicators.note: various suggests the letters come in assorted arrangements, so they are shuffled

parts.note: bob was slang for a shilling, abbreviated S in old British money

explanation.surface: A crowd of assorted old women plus an elderly man named Bob has gathered.
explanation.walkthrough: A beldame is an old woman; 'Bob' looks like a man's name but is slang for a shilling, the pre-decimal British coin, written S.
explanation.definitionFit: Assembled people have come together in one place, collected as a group.

clue.text: Bowl of food made from milk

explanation.surface: Someone offers a dish of dairy food.
explanation.walkthrough: In skittles, a game of knocking down pins, the heavy flat disc thrown at them is called a cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: In skittles the thrown disc carries that name; and the second sense is the familiar dairy product of curdled milk.

clue.text: Rex needs a shallow container for the plant

parts.note: Rex, Latin for king, is abbreviated R
a dish is a shallow vessel for food

explanation.surface: A king called Rex wants a shallow pot for a plant.
explanation.definitionFit: The radish is a garden vegetable grown for its peppery root, so it is a plant.

clue.text: Freedom to return again to the path

parts.note: the prefix re- means again
a course is a route or path taken

explanation.surface: Someone is free to go back to the trail again.
explanation.definitionFit: Recourse is a resort to some source of help, the right to fall back on it when needed.

clue.text: Hazel to finish first cake

indicators.note: to finish places the hazel piece at the end, after the other piece

parts.note: do (doh) is the first note of the sol-fa scale
the hazel bears a nut, the hazelnut

explanation.surface: Hazel wants to finish off the first cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hazel' looks like a woman's name but is the tree's nut; 'first' is DO, the first note of the sol-fa scale.
explanation.definitionFit: A ring-shaped fried sweet bun, spelt doughnut or donut, is a small cake.

clue.text: Suitable for use in the main

definitions.text: Suitable for use in the main

parts.words: Suitable for use in the main
parts.note: the main is an old poetic term for the open ocean, so this describes something built for ocean voyages

explanation.walkthrough: 'The main' looks like a pipe or chief thing, but is the poetic term for the high sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A vessel fit for ocean travel is described as built to go out on the waves.

clue.text: Rescues post and avoids imminent disaster

explanation.surface: A rescuer keeps a job going and heads off a catastrophe.
explanation.definitionFit: Read literally, the phrase means rescuing one's position or job; idiomatically it means preventing a crisis at the last moment.

clue.text: Play school syllabus is a disgrace

explanation.surface: A school's drama course is described as shameful.
explanation.walkthrough: Sheridan's comedy is The School for Scandal, so the play's school teaches this subject.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheridan's comedy title is The School for Scandal, so that school teaches it; and a public outrage or shame is the second sense.

clue.text: Remove the written evidence

parts.note: reads like a cover-up of documents, but simply describes rubbing out writing

explanation.definitionFit: To rub out marks with a rubber wipes away what was written.

clue.text: See 8
Numismatist's theory?

indicators.note: the possessive 's marks that the word has the letters within it

explanation.surface: A coin collector has a pet theory.
explanation.definitionFit: An ism is a doctrine or system of belief, a theory as the clue puts it.

clue.text: See 30 across
Descendants, boys going round Jersey and Guernsey

indicators.note: going round means the boys' letters wrap the islands' letters

parts.note: sons are boys
these are Channel Islands, abbreviated CI

explanation.surface: Young heirs are sailing round the Channel Islands.
explanation.walkthrough: Jersey and Guernsey are the main Channel Islands, off the French coast, abbreviated CI.
explanation.definitionFit: Scions are heirs or offspring of a family line.

clue.text: A box of matches?

parts.note: a box of matches is usually a small carton of matchsticks; here it is a box of things that do the same job of lighting

explanation.walkthrough: 'Matches' here means equals: a box of items equivalent to matches, used to light smokes.
explanation.definitionFit: Gas or flint lighters for smokes do the job matches do, so a box of them is a box of matches in another sense.

clue.text: See 15
Go down at sea

parts.note: reads like a ship sinking, but describes the tide falling back

explanation.definitionFit: The ebb is the outgoing tide, when the sea level falls.

clue.text: Levity unsuitable for the elderly

parts.note: something bad is unsuitable
in age means in old age, describing the elderly

explanation.surface: Joking around is thought inappropriate for old people.
explanation.definitionFit: Badinage is playful banter, light-hearted joking talk.

clue.text: Romanian money used for Hawaiian wreath

explanation.surface: Romanian cash pays for a Hawaiian garland.
explanation.definitionFit: The leu is Romania's currency unit, with this plural; and a garland of flowers given in Hawaii is the second sense.

clue.text: Bounder in American intelligence unit finds an insect

indicators.note: in places the bounder inside the agency's letters

parts.note: the CIA is the US Central Intelligence Agency
a cad or bounder is a dishonourable man

explanation.surface: A rogue agent in the US spy service discovers a bug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bounder' is old British slang for a cad, not something that bounds; the insect is a chirping cicada.
explanation.definitionFit: The cicada is a loud chirping bug of warm climates.

clue.text: Lady is a devout woman who is not socially acceptable

indicators.note: not means the socially acceptable letter is taken away

parts.note: a nun is a woman in holy orders
U means upper-class or socially acceptable in British usage

explanation.surface: A lady is a religious woman who is shunned by society.
explanation.walkthrough: U and non-U were British labels for upper-class and non-upper-class usage, so U means socially acceptable.
explanation.definitionFit: A girl's name stands for a lady, as crossword setters often use a woman's name this way.

clue.text: Wanderer who made progress according to the book

definitions.text: Wanderer who made progress according to the book

parts.words: Wanderer who made progress according to the book
parts.note: alludes to Bunyan's allegory of a traveller's progress toward the Celestial City

explanation.definitionFit: John Bunyan's book The Pilgrim's Progress follows a traveller on a religious journey.

clue.text: Denial, say, in the country

indicators.note: in places the example's letters inside the country's

parts.note: a nation is a country
say signals an example, e.g.

explanation.surface: Someone says no to something happening in their homeland.
explanation.definitionFit: A refusal or contradiction is a denial, the act of saying no.

clue.text: Another girl from Hester

indicators.note: another suggests a different arrangement of the name's letters

explanation.surface: A second girl comes from a woman called Hester.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's first name, from the biblical queen, stands for a girl.

clue.text: Could have gone round North America during period of immaturity

indicators.note: round means the rearranged letters wrap the abbreviation
could have suggests the word may be in another form, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone might have toured America while still young.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Could have' rearranges GONE to NOGE, and 'round' puts it around NA.
explanation.definitionFit: Nonage is the legal state of being under age, a minority.

clue.text: Mixing Spanish and French players

indicators.note: mixing means the letters are stirred together into a new order

parts.note: et is French for and

explanation.surface: A cast blends Spanish and French actors.
explanation.definitionFit: Thespians are actors, named after Thespis, the legendary first actor of Greek drama.

clue.text: The place in Italy to have an anise cocktail?

indicators.note: a cocktail is a mix, so the letters are blended into a new order

explanation.surface: A tourist wonders where in Italy to drink an aniseed cocktail.
explanation.definitionFit: A Tuscan hill city famous for its Palio horse race is a place in Italy.

clue.text: Without gravity, river flows back in Scotland

indicators.note: without here means outside, so the turned river surrounds the gravity letter
flows back means the river is read backwards

parts.note: the Nile is the African river
G is the symbol for gravity in physics

explanation.surface: Weightless, a river runs backwards somewhere in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' is the old sense outside, not lacking: ELIN goes around G.
explanation.definitionFit: Elgin is a town in Moray in north-east Scotland, a place in Scotland.

clue.text: Officer involving everyone

explanation.surface: An army officer includes all the troops.
explanation.definitionFit: A senior army rank is the first sense; and the adjective meaning widespread, affecting all, is the second.

clue.text: Initial problems experienced by babies

explanation.surface: Babies suffer early difficulties.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiomatically the phrase means early snags in a new project; literally it is the discomfort infants feel as teeth come through.

clue.text: Piece of land 'e 'as attached to the gallery

parts.note: dropped aitches turn he has into 'e's, giving the letters E and S
the Tate is the London art gallery

explanation.surface: A Cockney says his plot of land is beside the art gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney speech drops the h, so he has becomes 'e 'as, contracted to E'S; the Tate is a London gallery.
explanation.definitionFit: An estate is a large area of land owned by one person or family.
